HEALTH CARE SURROGATE DECISION-MAKING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe

HEALTH CARE SURROGATE DECISION-MAKING — INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet explains California's statutory scheme, set out in Probate Code Chapter 3 of the Health Care Decisions Law (Prob. Code §§ 4711-4717), for who may make health care decisions for a patient who currently lacks the capacity to make them personally. It covers the informal, provider-recorded oral surrogate designation a patient with capacity may make under § 4711; the descending statutory order of priority among a § 4711 surrogate, an agent under a power of attorney for health care or advance health care directive, and a conservator or guardian under § 4712(a); the separate process by which a health care provider or facility designee may choose a surrogate under § 4712(b) when none of those decisionmakers exists; the decision-making standard a surrogate must apply under § 4714; a patient's right to disqualify a person from serving as surrogate under § 4715; domestic-partner parity under § 4716; and a hospital emergency department's contact-effort duty under § 4717. This sheet does not create, execute, or record a surrogate designation, an advance health care directive, or a power of attorney for health care — Jane Doe is described here in the general terms the statute uses, without this sheet determining who Jane Doe's decisionmaker is, will be, or should be in any actual situation. It is distinct from this corpus's existing Advance Health Care Directive document (which lets a person execute a written directive naming an agent) and its existing Individual Health Care Instruction document (which lets a person record wishes directly without naming any agent or surrogate) — this sheet instead explains the fallback statutory framework that determines who may decide when no such written instrument, or no effective one, controls the moment. This sheet states facts about California law generally. It is not legal advice, and it does not determine who has authority to make a health care decision for any specific patient, in any specific hospital or facility, at any specific moment — that determination depends on facts (capacity, existing documents, family relationships, provider assessments) that only apply to one real situation at a time.

A PATIENT MAY DESIGNATE AN ORAL SURROGATE DIRECTLY TO A HEALTH CARE PROVIDER
California law lets a patient designate an adult as a health care surrogate without any written instrument, simply by personally informing the supervising health care provider or a designee of the health care facility caring for the patient; that designation must then be promptly recorded in the patient's health care record. This is a separate, lighter-weight mechanism from executing a power of attorney for health care or advance health care directive, and it exists specifically for use within a course of treatment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A patient may designate an adult as a surrogate to make health care decisions by personally informing the supervising health care provider or a designee of the health care facility caring for the patient. The designation of a surrogate shall be promptly recorded in the patient’s health care record."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4711(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the oral surrogate designation mechanism (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4711.)
  Known gap: This clause describes only how a § 4711 surrogate designation is made — it does not state or determine how long any particular designation lasts (covered in a separate clause on § 4711(b)'s time limit), what decisions the surrogate may make, or whether a specific health care provider's recording of a specific designation was done correctly. It also does not address a facility's own internal documentation forms or policies, which the statute does not standardize.

A § 4711 SURROGATE DESIGNATION IS TIME-LIMITED AND ONLY TEMPORARILY OUTRANKS AN AGENT
A surrogate designation made under § 4711 is not permanent. Unless the patient specifies a shorter period, it lasts only for the course of the treatment or illness, or the stay in the health care institution, during which it was made, or 60 days — whichever of those is shorter. During that limited period, if the patient has also designated an agent under a power of attorney for health care, the surrogate has priority over the agent notwithstanding the general rule (stated in a separate section, § 4685) that a reasonably available, willing agent otherwise has priority over any other person. But making a surrogate designation does not itself revoke the agent's designation — the agent's authority resumes once the surrogate designation expires, unless the patient separately communicates an intent to revoke the agent designation in the manner § 4695(a) requires (a signed writing or personally informing the supervising health care provider).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Unless the patient specifies a shorter period, a surrogate designation under subdivision (a) is effective only during the course of treatment or illness or during the stay in the health care institution when the surrogate designation is made, or for 60 days, whichever period is shorter."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4711(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the time limit on a surrogate designation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4711.)
  "Notwithstanding Section 4685, if the patient has designated an agent under a power of attorney for health care, the surrogate designated under subdivision (a) has priority over the agent for the period provided in subdivision (b), but the designation of a surrogate does not revoke the designation of an agent unless the patient communicates the intention to revoke in compliance with subdivision (a) of Section 4695."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4711(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, a surrogate's temporary priority over an agent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4711.)
  "Unless the power of attorney for health care provides otherwise, the agent designated in the power of attorney who is known to the health care provider to be reasonably available and willing to make health care decisions has priority over any other person in making health care decisions for the principal."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4685 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the general rule that a reasonably available agent has priority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4685.)
  Known gap: This clause states the duration and priority rules § 4711 itself sets out — it does not determine whether a specific patient's designation has expired at a given moment, whether a specific provider correctly treated a designation as still in effect, or whether a specific patient's later statements amounted to a revocation of an agent's designation under § 4695(a). The interaction described here is between a § 4711 surrogate and an agent specifically; it does not address how a surrogate designation interacts with a conservator's or guardian's authority, which a separate clause on § 4712(a)'s priority order covers.

THE STATUTORY ORDER OF PRIORITY AMONG LEGALLY RECOGNIZED DECISIONMAKERS
When a patient lacks the capacity to make a health care decision, California law sets a descending order of priority among the decisionmakers it recognizes: first, a surrogate the patient selected under § 4711; second, an agent under an advance health care directive or a power of attorney for health care; and third, a conservator or guardian of the patient who has authority over health care decisions. This order determines which recognized decisionmaker's decision controls when more than one such decisionmaker exists for the same patient at the same time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If a patient lacks the capacity to make a health care decision, the following legally recognized health care decisionmakers may make health care decisions on the patient’s behalf, in the following descending order of priority:(1) The patient’s surrogate selected pursuant to Section 4711.(2) The patient’s agent pursuant to an advance health care directive or a power of attorney for health care.(3) The conservator or guardian of the patient having the authority to make health care decisions for the patient."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4712(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the descending priority order of health care decisionmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4712.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the three-tier order the statute sets among decisionmakers who already qualify under one of its three categories — it does not determine whether a specific person actually qualifies as a valid § 4711 surrogate, agent, or conservator/guardian in a given case, and it does not address what happens when none of the three exists (covered in a separate clause on § 4712(b)'s provider-selected surrogate process). A CourtListener case-law search for judicial interpretation of this priority order returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, quota exhausted) before any results could be reviewed, so this clause rests on the statutory text alone and does not reflect whether courts have construed this ordering in any reported decision.

WHEN NO RECOGNIZED DECISIONMAKER EXISTS, A PROVIDER MAY CHOOSE A SURROGATE FROM AN ENUMERATED LIST
California law does not automatically hand health care decision-making authority to a next of kin simply because a patient lacks capacity and has no surrogate, agent, conservator, or guardian. Instead, in that situation, a health care provider or a designee of the health care facility caring for the patient may choose a surrogate, as appropriate to the situation. The person chosen must be an adult who has demonstrated special care and concern for the patient, is familiar with the patient's personal values and beliefs to the extent known, and is reasonably available and willing to serve. The statute lists categories from which that surrogate may be chosen, in the order given: a spouse or domestic partner, an adult child, a parent, an adult sibling, an adult grandchild, or an adult relative or close personal friend. This selection is subject to any disqualification the patient made under § 4715 while the patient still had capacity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as set forth in Section 4715, if a patient lacks the capacity to make a health care decision, but does not have a legally recognized health care decisionmaker pursuant to subdivision (a), a health care provider or a designee of the health care facility caring for the patient may choose a surrogate to make health care decisions on the patient’s behalf, as appropriate in the given situation. The patient’s surrogate shall be an adult who has demonstrated special care and concern for the patient, is familiar with the patient’s personal values and beliefs to the extent known, and is reasonably available and willing to serve. A surrogate may be chosen from any of the following persons:(1) The spouse or domestic partner of the patient.(2) An adult child of the patient.(3) A parent of the patient.(4) An adult sibling of the patient.(5) An adult grandchild of the patient.(6) An adult relative or close personal friend."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4712(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the provider-selected surrogate process and eligible categories (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4712.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the qualifying standard and the list of eligible categories the statute sets — it does not determine that any specific person meets that standard for any specific patient, does not resolve a dispute among family members over who should be chosen, and does not address California's separate, more procedurally detailed surrogate decision-making rules for skilled nursing facility residents under Health & Safety Code § 1418.8, which this sheet was not researched to cover and does not describe.

THE STANDARD A SURROGATE MUST APPLY IN DECIDING
A surrogate does not decide freely. California law requires a surrogate (including a person acting as a surrogate) to make a health care decision in accordance with the patient's own individual health care instructions, if any, and the patient's other wishes to the extent the surrogate knows them. Only if the patient's wishes are not known does the surrogate decide according to the surrogate's determination of the patient's best interest — and even then, the surrogate must consider the patient's personal values to the extent known.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A surrogate, including a person acting as a surrogate, shall make a health care decision in accordance with the patient’s individual health care instructions, if any, and other wishes to the extent known to the surrogate. Otherwise, the surrogate shall make the decision in accordance with the surrogate’s determination of the patient’s best interest. In determining the patient’s best interest, the surrogate shall consider the patient’s personal values to the extent known to the surrogate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4714 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the surrogate's decision-making standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4714.)
  Known gap: This clause states the legal standard itself — it does not determine what a specific patient's wishes or values actually were, whether a specific surrogate correctly applied this standard in a specific decision, or how a dispute over what the standard requires in a given case would be resolved. A CourtListener search for case law interpreting this substituted-judgment/best-interest standard returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) before any case could be reviewed, so no judicial gloss on this standard is reflected here.

A PATIENT MAY DISQUALIFY A SPECIFIC PERSON FROM EVER ACTING AS SURROGATE
While a patient still has capacity, California law lets that patient disqualify another person — including a member of the patient's own family — from acting as the patient's surrogate. This can be done at any time, either by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider of the disqualification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A patient having capacity at any time may disqualify another person, including a member of the patient’s family, from acting as the patient’s surrogate by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider of the disqualification."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4715 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, a patient's right to disqualify a person from serving as surrogate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4715.)
  Known gap: This clause states only that the disqualification right exists and how it may be exercised — it does not determine whether a specific communication to a specific provider was sufficient to accomplish a disqualification, how a disqualification is recorded or verified afterward, or whether a disqualified person might still qualify to act under some other legal authority (such as a later-appointed conservatorship) that this statute does not reach.

A REGISTERED DOMESTIC PARTNER HAS THE SAME AUTHORITY AS A SPOUSE
California law gives a patient's domestic partner the same authority a spouse has to make a health care decision for an incapacitated partner, when the patient lacks capacity. The statute is explicit that it does not expand or restrict a spouse's own existing authority to make health care decisions for an incapacitated spouse — it equalizes the domestic partner's position with whatever the spousal rule already is, rather than creating a new or different rule.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If a patient lacks the capacity to make a health care decision, the patient’s domestic partner shall have the same authority as a spouse has to make a health care decision for his or her incapacitated spouse. This section may not be construed to expand or restrict the ability of a spouse to make a health care decision for an incapacitated spouse."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4716(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, domestic-partner parity with a spouse's health care decision-making authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4716.)
  Known gap: This clause states only that domestic-partner parity exists as a matter of statute — it does not itself state what a spouse's authority to make health care decisions for an incapacitated spouse consists of in any given circumstance (that depends on the other provisions of this same statutory scheme, including the priority order and decision standard covered in this sheet's other clauses), and it does not determine whether a specific relationship qualifies as a domestic partnership within the meaning the statute cross-references.

A HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT'S 24-HOUR DUTY TO ATTEMPT CONTACT
California law imposes a specific, time-bound duty on a general acute care hospital: within 24 hours of the arrival in its emergency department of a patient who is unconscious or otherwise incapable of communication, the hospital must make reasonable efforts to contact the patient's agent, surrogate, or a family member or other person the hospital reasonably believes has authority to make health care decisions for the patient. The statute also describes specific steps — examining personal effects and medical records, contacting the identified person, and checking the Advance Health Care Directive Registry when there is evidence of a registry card — that, if all performed, are deemed to satisfy this duty, and requires the hospital to document its efforts in the patient's medical record. This duty is suspended while the hospital is operating under its own disaster and mass-casualty or fire and internal disaster program.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "within 24 hours of the arrival in the emergency department of a general acute care hospital of a patient who is unconscious or otherwise incapable of communication, the hospital shall make reasonable efforts to contact the patient’s agent, surrogate, or a family member or other person the hospital reasonably believes has the authority to make health care decisions on behalf of the patient."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4717(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, a hospital emergency department's duty to attempt contacting a decisionmaker (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4717.)
  Known gap: This clause states the hospital's duty to attempt contact — it does not determine that any specific hospital did or did not make reasonable efforts in a specific case, does not itself grant the contacted person decision-making authority (that depends on the priority-order and provider-selection rules covered in this sheet's other clauses), and does not apply outside a general acute care hospital's emergency department (it does not, for example, describe any comparable duty for other kinds of health care facilities).

CERTIFICATION OF UNDERSTANDING
I, Jane Doe, certify that I have read this information sheet describing California's statutory scheme for who may make health care decisions on behalf of a patient who currently lacks capacity, including the oral surrogate designation process, the statutory priority order among decisionmakers, the process for a provider-selected surrogate, the decision-making standard a surrogate must apply, the disqualification right, domestic-partner parity, and a hospital emergency department's contact duty. I understand that this sheet states facts about California law generally, that it is not legal advice, and that it does not determine who is or will be authorized to make a health care decision for me, or for anyone else, in any specific situation.

citations.quote: within 24 hours of the arrival in the emergency department of a general acute care hospital of a patient who is unconscious or otherwise incapable of communication, the hospital shall make reasonable efforts to contact the patient’s agent, surrogate, or a family member or other person the hospital reasonably believes has the authority to make health care decisions on behalf of the patient.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the hospital's duty to attempt contact — it does not determine that any specific hospital did or did not make reasonable efforts in a specific case, does not itself grant the contacted person decision-making authority (that depends on the priority-order and provider-selection rules covered in this sheet's other clauses), and does not apply outside a general acute care hospital's emergency department (it does not, for example, describe any comparable duty for other kinds of health care facilities).

expectedJSON.body: I, Jane Doe, certify that I have read this information sheet describing California's statutory scheme for who may make health care decisions on behalf of a patient who currently lacks capacity, including the oral surrogate designation process, the statutory priority order among decisionmakers, the process for a provider-selected surrogate, the decision-making standard a surrogate must apply, the disqualification right, domestic-partner parity, and a hospital emergency department's contact duty. I understand that this sheet states facts about California law generally, that it is not legal advice, and that it does not determine who is or will be authorized to make a health care decision for me, or for anyone else, in any specific situation.
